label: Passage Mapping
oneLiner: Read for structure: label each paragraph’s function and how it connects.
definition: Elite RC readers do not memorize details; they build a map—each paragraph’s job (background, thesis, counterargument, evidence, conclusion) and the links between them—then return to the text for specifics.
objectives: Label each paragraph’s function in a few words
Identify the author’s thesis and where it appears
Use the map to answer structure and function questions

examples.text: Reading a contract by its headings before its clauses.
Briefing a case: facts, issue, holding, reasoning.
Skimming an equity research report for thesis, catalysts, risks.

attack: Read ¶1 for topic and the “old view”
correctLooksLike: A paragraph-by-paragraph map: function + gist + links, plus the author’s thesis.
traps: Missing the pivot to the author’s view
commonError: Reading every detail with equal attention and losing the thread.

keyPoints.point: Return to the text for specifics

card.front: What are the five common paragraph functions?
card.back: Background, thesis, counterargument, evidence, author’s conclusion (plus concession, example, rebuttal).

label: Viewpoints
chapter: CHAPTER VII — THE CAST OF CHARACTERS
oneLiner: Track who believes what—and which voice is the author’s.
definition: Passages present multiple perspectives: traditional scholars, critics, defenders, the author. Questions test whether you can attribute views correctly.
objectives: Separate the author’s view from reported views

examples.text: A dinner-party argument: who said what?
A judicial opinion reporting each party’s argument before the court’s holding.
An analyst note quoting bulls and bears before the analyst’s rating.

attack: Name each viewpoint in two words
correctLooksLike: A cast list: each group, its stance, and its relation to the author.
traps: Attributing a reported view to the author
commonError: Answering with a view the author reports but rejects.

card.back: Attributing a view the author reports (and rejects) to the author.

label: Author’s Tone
oneLiner: Place the author on the scale from strongly negative to strongly positive.
definition: LSAT authors are rarely extreme. Tone answers usually combine a direction and a measured intensity: “qualified admiration,” “cautious skepticism.”

examples.text: “The plan is ambitious, if somewhat optimistic” — qualified approval.
“The doctrine’s prominence far outstrips its footing” — measured skepticism.
“A promising but unproven strategy” — cautious optimism.

correctLooksLike: A moderate, two-part description matching the author’s evaluative language.
traps: Neutral when the author clearly evaluates
commonError: Choosing an extreme tone because the author disagrees.

card.front: Why are “contempt” and “unbridled enthusiasm” rarely correct?
card.back: LSAT authors are measured; tone answers are usually moderate.

label: Comparative Passages
oneLiner: Map Passage A against Passage B: where they agree, disagree, and differ in scope.
definition: Comparative sets pair two shorter passages on a shared topic. Questions ask about relationships: what both address, what they’d agree or disagree on, and how one would respond to the other.
objectives: Build a two-circle Venn of the passages
Answer agree/disagree questions by testing both authors

examples.text: Two restaurant reviews of the same place.
Majority and dissenting opinions in the same case.
A bull and a bear note on the same stock.

attack: Fill the Venn: agree / disagree / A only / B only
Answer each question by testing both passages
correctLooksLike: A Venn diagram listing agreements, disagreements, and scope differences.
traps: Answers true of only one passage
commonError: Assuming Passage B responds directly to Passage A.

card.front: Common trap in “relationship between passages” questions?
card.back: “Directly rebuts/responds”—most comparative passages were written independently.

label: Structure: Theory & Critique
oneLiner: A view is presented, then critiqued—often with a qualified conclusion.
definition: The most common LSAT structure: a theory or traditional account, objections to it, sometimes a defense, and the author’s verdict.
objectives: Predict where the author’s verdict will appear

examples.text: A film review that summarizes praise, then dissents.
The persistent objector passage: doctrine → thin authority → rebuttal of defenders → verdict.
An article on an investing rule of thumb, followed by evidence that it fails.

traps: Mistaking the theory for the author’s view

card.front: Typical shape of a theory–critique passage?
card.back: Theory → critique → (defense) → the author’s (often qualified) verdict.

label: Structure: Problem & Solution
oneLiner: A problem is described; solutions are weighed; one is endorsed.
definition: Problem–solution passages describe a difficulty, evaluate approaches, and often recommend one.
objectives: Identify the problem and each proposed solution
Find the author’s preferred solution and its limits

examples.text: A city’s traffic problem and three proposed fixes.
Central bank mandates: problem of distributive decisions; solution: legislated mandates and oversight.
A company’s liquidity crunch and financing options.

attack: Note the author’s verdict on each
traps: Confusing a rejected solution with the endorsed one
commonError: Missing the qualification on the endorsed solution.

card.back: Problem → candidate solutions → the author’s recommended (often qualified) solution.

label: Structure: Old View, New View
oneLiner: A traditional understanding is revised by newer scholarship.
definition: Old-view/new-view passages describe a received account and the scholarship that revises it—often with the author adjusting the revision.
objectives: Separate old view, new view, and author

examples.text: “For years, nutritionists warned against all fats…”
The law merchant: traditional uniform law → revisionist critique → synthesis.
“The efficient-market view once dominated; behavioral finance revised it.”

attack: Locate the author relative to both
correctLooksLike: Old view → new view → author’s position.
traps: Assuming the author fully adopts the new view
commonError: Missing that the author qualifies the revision.

card.front: Signal phrases for an old-view/new-view passage?

label: Structure: Phenomenon & Explanation
oneLiner: A phenomenon is described; hypotheses to explain it are weighed.
definition: Common in science passages: an observation, competing explanations, evidence for and against each, and the author’s assessment.
objectives: Identify what evidence would distinguish them

examples.text: Why the dog barks at night: hunger, noise, or habit?
Why yields rose after a rate cut: inflation expectations vs. risk premia.
The wood-wide web: observed carbon movement, contested routes.

commonError: Treating a popular hypothesis as established.

card.front: In phenomenon–explanation passages, what do weaken/strengthen questions usually target?
card.back: Evidence that discriminates between competing hypotheses.

label: RC Main Point
definition: Main Point answers capture the author’s thesis and the passage’s scope—neither too narrow nor too broad.
objectives: Recognize RC Main Point questions from the stem

examples.text: A friend asks what a film was about—not what happened in scene three.
A case’s holding, not a footnote, is its main point.
An analyst note’s rating and thesis, not page 12’s revenue table.

attack: Prefer answers including the author’s verdict
traps: Reported views mistaken for the thesis

keyPoints.point: Avoid: Answers covering only one paragraph

children.label: Prefer answers including the author’s verdict
Reported views mistaken for the thesis

card.front: Two tests for an RC Main Point answer?
card.back: It states the author’s thesis and fits the scope of the entire passage.

label: Primary Purpose
oneLiner: Describe what the author is trying to DO.
definition: Primary Purpose answers start with a verb (evaluate, argue, describe, challenge) that must match the passage’s moves.
objectives: Recognize Primary Purpose questions from the stem

examples.text: A recipe’s purpose is to instruct; a restaurant review’s is to evaluate.
A dissent’s purpose is to challenge the majority’s reasoning.
A prospectus describes; an activist letter argues for change.

attack: Check every part of the answer
Match the author’s level of commitment
correctLooksLike: Match the author’s level of commitment

keyPoints.point: Describe what the author is trying to DO.
Avoid: Verbs that are too strong (“prove”, “refute”)

children.label: Describe what the author is trying to DO
Check every part of the answer
Match the author’s level of commitment

card.front: Why do Primary Purpose answers hinge on the verb?
card.back: The verb must match what the author actually does (describe vs. argue vs. evaluate).

label: Author’s Attitude
oneLiner: Identify the author’s stance and its intensity.
definition: Attitude answers combine direction and degree. Use the Tone Meter.
objectives: Recognize Author’s Attitude questions from the stem

examples.text: “The plan is bold, if a little optimistic” = qualified approval.
“The doctrine’s prominence far outstrips its footing” = measured skepticism.
“A promising but unproven strategy” = cautious optimism.

traps: Neutral answers when the author evaluates

keyPoints.point: Identify the author’s stance and its intensity.

children.label: Identify the author’s stance and its int
Neutral answers when the author evaluates

card.back: Moderate and often two-part, e.g. “qualified admiration”.

label: Detail
oneLiner: Find what the passage explicitly says.
definition: Detail questions reward locating the line, not remembering it.
objectives: Recognize Detail questions from the stem

examples.text: Checking the ticket for the departure time instead of guessing.
Quoting the statute’s text rather than recalling it.
Pulling the exact covenant figure from the credit agreement.

attack: Use your map to locate the paragraph
traps: True statements from the wrong paragraph

keyPoints.point: Find what the passage explicitly says.
Avoid: Answers that distort a detail

children.label: Find what the passage explicitly says.
Use your map to locate the paragraph
True statements from the wrong paragraph

card.back: Go back to the text and find the line; match the paraphrase.

label: Inference
oneLiner: Find what the passage supports without stating.
definition: Inference answers are one small step from the text—supported, not speculative.
objectives: Recognize Inference questions from the stem

examples.text: Wet umbrella + soaked coat → it was raining outside.
A court calling remarks “dicta” implies they did not decide the case.
A CFO hedging every guidance figure suggests uncertainty about next quarter.

keyPoints.point: Find what the passage supports without stating.

children.label: Find what the passage supports without s

card.front: How big a step is an RC inference?
card.back: One small, well-supported step from specific text.

label: Function
oneLiner: Explain why a detail or paragraph is there.
definition: Function questions ask the purpose of a word, example, or paragraph within the author’s argument.
objectives: Recognize Function questions from the stem

examples.text: A joke in a toast exists to relax the room.
A hypothetical in an opinion illustrates the rule’s limits.
A sensitivity table in a model shows how fragile the valuation is.

attack: Ask: what does this help the author do?
correctLooksLike: Ask: what does this help the author do?

keyPoints.point: Explain why a detail or paragraph is there.
Avoid: Describing content rather than purpose

children.label: Explain why a detail or paragraph is the
Ask: what does this help the author do?

card.back: Function asks WHY something is there; Detail asks WHAT is said.

label: Analogy
oneLiner: Match the passage’s situation to an abstract parallel.
definition: Analogy questions require stripping the situation to its relationships and matching another situation with the same structure.
objectives: Recognize Analogy questions from the stem

examples.text: A thermostat is to a furnace as a conductor is to an orchestra (controller → performer).
A precedent is to a court as a map is to a traveler (guide, not destination).
A covenant is to a loan as a guardrail is to a road.

keyPoints.point: Match the passage’s situation to an abstract parallel.

children.label: Match the passage’s situation to an abst

card.front: First step on RC Analogy questions?
card.back: State the relationship abstractly, ignoring the subject matter.

label: Structure
oneLiner: Describe how the passage is organized.
definition: Structure answers must match every paragraph, in order—use your map.
objectives: Recognize Structure questions from the stem

examples.text: A sermon: text, exposition, application.
A judicial opinion: facts, issue, holding, reasoning.
A pitch book: situation, options, recommendation.

attack: Lay your map beside each answer
traps: Answers with an extra or missing step
commonError: Answers with an extra or missing step

keyPoints.point: Describe how the passage is organized.
Avoid: Answers with an extra or missing step

children.label: Describe how the passage is organized.
Lay your map beside each answer
Answers with an extra or missing step

card.front: How do you verify a Structure answer?
card.back: Match each clause, in order, to your paragraph map.

label: RC Strengthen / Weaken
oneLiner: Find new information that helps or hurts a claim in the passage.
definition: Like LR Strengthen/Weaken, but the argument lives in a passage. Identify whose claim and what evidence it rests on.
objectives: Recognize RC Strengthen / Weaken questions from the stem

examples.text: A restaurant critic’s claim weakened by learning the chef was absent that night.
Evidence that tribunals applied a doctrine weakens a claim that it is never applied.
Learning a fund’s returns came from leverage weakens a skill claim.

attack: Choose the answer that hits the gap
correctLooksLike: Choose the answer that hits the gap

keyPoints.point: Find new information that helps or hurts a claim in the passage.

children.label: Find new information that helps or hurts
Choose the answer that hits the gap

card.back: Identify exactly whose claim is being strengthened or weakened.

label: Comparative Relationship
oneLiner: Relate Passage A to Passage B.
definition: Comparative questions test agreements, disagreements, and how one author would respond to the other.
objectives: Recognize Comparative Relationship questions from the stem

examples.text: Two reviews of the same play: what both praise, where they split.
Majority and dissent: shared facts, opposite holdings.
Bull and bear notes on one stock: same data, different weighting.

attack: Test each answer against BOTH passages

keyPoints.point: Relate Passage A to Passage B.

children.label: Relate Passage A to Passage B.
Test each answer against BOTH passages

card.back: Test each answer against BOTH passages.
